title: Multi-omics and machine learning-driven CD8 + T cell heterogeneity score for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

sections.abstract:
The heterogeneity of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) poses a significant challenge to treatment, underscoring the urgent need for more precise and personalized therapeutic approaches. CD8 + T cells, integral components of the tumor immune microenvironment, have emerged as key targets for immunotherapy. Our research has established a correlation between a decrease in CD8 + T cell score and a poor clinical prognosis, highlighting the prognostic value of this biomarker. By analyzing the gene expression related to CD8 + T cells, we have differentiated HNSCC into cold and hot tumor subtypes, uncovering disparities in clinical prognosis and responses to immunotherapy. Utilizing eight machine learning methods, we identified the key gene OLR1. Single-cell analysis of HNSCC tissues and peripheral blood, along with spatial transcriptome analysis, revealed that OLR1 predominantly functions in macrophages, modulating the immune microenvironment of HNSCC. The expression level of OLR1 may serve as a predictive marker for immunotherapy responses. Moreover, drug sensitivity analysis and molecular docking studies have indicated that simvastatin and pazopanib are potential inhibitors of OLR1. These findings suggest that simvastatin and pazopanib could open up innovative potential therapeutic avenues for individuals with HNSCC.

Keywords: MT: Bioinformatics, HNSCC, CD8 + T cells, multi-omics, machine learning, precision therapy, OLR1
sections.introduction:
According to the Global Cancer Report, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is the seventh most prevalent cancer globally and affects the mucosal epithelium of the mouth, paranasal sinuses, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx. Approximately 900,000 new cases are diagnosed and 350,000 deaths occur annually worldwide, exhibiting a persistent increasing trend in recent years. 1 , 2 Presently, most cases of HNSCC are found to be regionally advanced, with lymph node spread upon diagnosis, posing a notable danger to human health. Untreated HNSCC is a comprehensive treatment option depending on the stage of the disease, including local surgical removal, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy. 3 , 4 HNSCC is a highly diverse and complex disease characterized by notable inter- and intra-tumor heterogeneity, and the response to current targeted therapy is poor; thus, its clinical prognosis remains unfavorable. More than half of the patients may experience local recurrence or distant metastasis after treatment, and the overall survival of patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC (R/M HNSCC) is less than 1 year. 5 , 6 Recently, immunotherapy has rapidly changed the treatment prospects for HNSCC, represented by immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) therapy, which has evolved from a second-line treatment method for R/M HNSCC to a first-line treatment method. 7 , 8 However, immunotherapy is only effective for selected patients due to various resistance mechanisms. Therefore, the heterogeneity of HNSCC must be explored, novel therapeutic targets must be identified, and the response to immunotherapy must be enhanced crucially to improve HNSCC prognosis.

One of the key features of tumors is an unbalanced tumor microenvironment (TME), which consists of various cell subpopulations, including adaptive immune cells, myeloid cells, tumor stromal cells, stromal components, and blood vessel cells. 9 The interactions between these cell subgroups and cytokines are essential for controlling immunosurveillance and managing tumor growth. Multiple studies have demonstrated that malfunctions in immune killer cells and the abnormal release of immune-related substances in the TME can lead to immunosuppression and advancement of HNSCC. 10 , 11 Specifically, CD8 + T cells, also referred to as cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), are essential components of the TME and play a crucial role in the immune response against tumors. 12 , 13 They can specifically recognize antigen peptide-major histocompatibility complex class I complexes and eliminate target cells, including intracellular pathogen-infected and tumor cells. The killing mechanisms involve perforin and granzyme secretion, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) expression, and induction of apoptosis through the FAS/FASL pathway. Numerous studies have indicated that a high infiltration of CD8 + T cells can serve as an important predictor for positive results and a crucial element in immune checkpoint blockade treatment. 14 , 15 Yang et al. further reported that the upregulation of hub gene YKT6, associated with lower CD8 + T cell infiltration, was linked to adverse prognosis in oral cancer. 16 However, our understanding of the controlling mechanisms and central genes associated with CD8 + T cell infiltration in HNSCC is still lacking. Therefore, a deeper understanding of the important genes related to CD8 + T cell immunity and the relationships between CD8 + T cells and other cell subgroups could reveal novel targets for immunotherapy in HNSCC.

Omics technology offers an efficient and rapid approach to uncovering intricate biological information related to human diseases. 17 , 18 Bulk transcriptomics involves all RNA transcribed by living cells, focusing on the regulation of transcription in cells as a whole and identifying key genes and disease subtypes. 19 Single-cell genomics focusing on a single cell has been utilized to investigate the TME, revealing key findings, such as significant heterogeneity, the functional range of tumor-infiltrating T cells, and intercellular interaction combined with the CellChat method. 20 For example, Huang et al. conducted thorough analyses of both bulk and single-cell transcriptomes to reveal the cellular structure and developmental paths of hepatoblastomas, while also identifying facilitates chromatin transcription inhibition as a promising targeted therapy. 21 Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technology can better observe cell location and heterogeneity in developing cell lineages, further providing information on intercellular communication at the spatial level. 22 Olaniru et al. demonstrated distinct gene cascades over time and space, as well as the co-location of two cell types by integrating single-cell transcriptomics and ST at various developmental stages. 23 Additionally, machine learning and deep learning models have been used recently for survival prediction and now support the decision process of clinicians. 24 Based on the aforementioned methods, we can completely explore the TME and intercellular communication in HNSCC, providing evidence for potential therapeutic targets.

In this study, we initially confirmed that the level of CD8 + T cell infiltration was closely linked to the outcome of HNSCC and identified significant genes related to CD8 + T cell infiltration through weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Molecular clusters based on CD8 + T cell immune-related genes in HNSCC were established to assess their correlation with biological functions, immune environments, and patient outcomes. We used a comprehensive method that involved various machine learning techniques to identify the hub gene OLR1 with prognosis. The expression of OLR-1 in tumor tissues was further validated using Real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analysis and immunohistochemistry (IHC). We then explored the expression of OLR1 and its correlation with immune checkpoint genes, immune score, and immunotherapy response and conducted a drug sensitivity analysis to identify potential targeted drugs. Additionally, we elucidated the signaling pathway between CD8 + T cells and myeloid immune cells in tissue specimens and peripheral blood based on single-cell analysis and ST data. We further found high OLR1 expression in M0 macrophages and explored the co-expression of OLR1 and apolipoprotein E (APOE) through immunofluorescence, suggesting that OLR-1 might regulate CD8 + T cell infiltration through signaling pathways between CD8 + T cells and macrophages via pseudotime analysis and CellChat. Overall, our findings lay the groundwork for a better understanding of significant CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes and potential signaling pathways between CD8 + T cells and other TME components, aiming at targeting tumor-specific cell-cell networks and improving the prognosis of HNSCC.
sections.methods:
Transcriptome data and clinicopathological features of 502 HNSCC patients and 44 normal samples were obtained from TCGA database (TCGA database: https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). Background adjustment and quantified normalization were performed on 518 HNSCC tumor samples from 4 eligible GEO datasets ( GSE65858 , GSE41613 , GSE42743 , and GSE117973 ) obtained from the GEO database (GEO database: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ). The E-MTAB-8588 dataset, which consists of 117 HNSCC samples and 98 normal samples, was obtained from the ArrayExpress database (ArrayExpress database: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/arrayexpress/ ). Samples lacking overall survival information were excluded. We finally obtained 1,048 HNSCC samples with complete transcriptome and clinical data. Data from single-cell RNA-seq were acquired from the GEO database, consisting of 26 samples of paired peripheral blood mononuclear cells and tumor-infiltrating immune cells from patients with HNSCC, 6 samples of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from healthy donors, and 5 samples of tissue resident immune cells from the tonsils of healthy donors. Data from ST were obtained from GSM5494482 (GEO database: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ).

DEGs were identified in TCGA cohort using the R package limma based on genes with a |log fold change| >0.5 and false discovery rate <0.05. A total of 4,203 DEGs from TCGA cohort were utilized in WGCNA to identify the key genes in the most significant module. The WGCNA analysis involved the use of R packages such as matrixStats, Hmisc, Foreach, doParways, fast cluster, DynamicTreeCut, Survival, and WGCNA. The ME purple modules genes’ PPI networks were obtained from STRING (STRING database: http://string-db.org ) and displayed using Gephi software.

Prognosis-related genes were identified in the entire TCGA cohort using univariable Cox regression analysis with a significance level of p < 0.05. The R package non-negative matrix factorization was employed to discover molecular clusters related to CD8 + T cells. Next, the groupings were confirmed through the use of PCA, UMAP, and t-SNE with the assistance of the R packages ggplot2, umap, and Rtsne. Visualization of gene expression in various clusters was performed with the R tool pheatmap.

To understand the pathways and functions related to genes associated with CD8 + T cells, we performed an analysis using the clusterprofiler package to examine GO and KEGG. 64 We considered adjusted p < 0.05 and q < 0.2 to be statistically significant. GSEA using KEGG and Hallmark genes was used to detect signaling pathways in various clusters, while GSVA enabled the evaluation of potential alterations in pathway activity across different clusters. 65 , 66

The TIDE algorithm from http://tide.dfci.harvard.edu was utilized to determine the TIDE score, which consists of a Dysfunction score and an Exclusion score. Additionally, the ssGSEA algorithm was employed to evaluate immune cell infiltration and immune-related functions. CIBERSORT, a deconvolution algorithm, was utilized to estimate the proportions of 22 tumor-infiltrating immune cells in tumor tissues with mixed cell types. ESTIMATE was used to estimate stromal and immune cells in malignant tumors, as well as calculate tumor purity, stromal score, immune score, and ESTIMATE score.

To determine the genes most linked to prognosis, we combined eight different machine learning algorithms: LASSO regression, RF, GB, KNN, SVM, GBM, XGBoost, and DT. All models were detected in 1,048 HNSCC samples with overall survival.

LASSO regression was performed using glmnt, generating candidate diagnostic genes through 10-fold cross-validation. The RF model was created using the randomForest package. GBM calculation was conducted using the gbm method from the caret R package. The XGBoost calculation was conducted using the xgbTree method from the caret R package. The DT calculation was performed using the rpart R package.

GB used the sklearn GradientBoostingClassifier ensemble module for training. KNN used the KNeighborsClassifier from sklearn.neighbors. SVM utilized the Support Vector Classifier (SVC) class of sklearn.svm module with a linear kernel. These three algorithms were implemented through Pathon (Python version 3.9.7; key libraries: scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn). To guarantee the strength and dependability of the outcomes, every machine learning model underwent training and validation through a 5-fold cross-validation process. The importance of each feature was determined using permutation importance, and the top 10 features were visualized and saved as PDF files for further analysis.

RNA-seq data and sample annotation information were obtained using the Seurat R package. To exclude low-quality cells and genes with low expression, the following thresholds were applied: (1) each gene had to be expressed in at least three cells; (2) the number of features per cell ranged from 200 to 5,000; and (3) the proportion of mitochondria was required to be less than 20%, and hemoglobin content in each cell was required to be less than 3%. Subsequently, data standardization was performed using the NormalizeData function, followed by the identification of highly variable genes based on average expression values (>0.125 and <3) and dispersion (>0.5), utilizing the FindVariableFeatures function. Batch correction between samples was conducted using the Harmony package in R to mitigate any batch effects that could interfere with downstream analysis. Finally, dimensionality reduction through PCA was employed after scaling the data, selecting the top 20 PCs for subsequent analysis.

ST data analysis was performed using the Seurat R package, employing methods similar to those used for single-cell RNA-seq data analysis. The FindTransferAnchors and TransferData functions, with default settings from the Seurat R package, were utilized to predict single-cell data on the ST data.

We employed the CellChat R package to explore the crosstalk pattern between cells. Following the prescribed procedure, we generated the CellChat entity using a standardized count matrix. We performed permutation tests to evaluate the statistical significance and used default on method parameters.

TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA) was utilized to extract mRNA from tumor tissue to confirm the dependability of potent prognostic genes in HNSCC patients and normal control tissue, respectively. The primers utilized for RT-qPCR analysis are outlined in Table S1 . The internal control utilized was glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase.

Formalin-fixed paraffin sections of HNSCC tissues underwent rehydration and antigen retrieval. The areas were obstructed using BSA and then exposed to primary anti-OLR-1 antibody as per the instructions provided by the manufacturer. Afterward, slides were exposed to a secondary antibody linked with horseradish peroxidase (Abcam, Cambridge, UK), detected using the 3,3′-diaminobenzidine method, stained with H&E, and dehydrated. Evaluation of the sections was performed under an optical microscope. The antibody used was anti-OLR1 (11837-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China).

We utilized BSA to block the paraffin sections, followed by an overnight incubation at 4°C in a humidified chamber with primary antibodies (anti-OLR1, anti-APOE). Subsequently, the slides were exposed to fluorescein-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature under dark conditions. To visualize nuclei, we employed DAPI as a counterstain. Imaging was performed using confocal microscopy from Nikon. The antibodies used were anti-OLR1 (11837-1-AP, Proteintech) and anti-APOE (18254-1-AP, Proteintech).

The Spearman correlation coefficients were calculated using the GSCALite 67 online database to examine the relationship between OLR1 expression levels and drug sensitivity (half-maximal inhibitory concentration [IC 50 ]) for 86 small-molecule drugs from the GDSC and CTRP databases. Predictions using molecular docking were conducted on https://www.dockeasy.cn/DockCompound . Molecular docking results were visualized using Discovery Studio version 4.5. The chemical compositions of the medication were acquired from https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/#query . Protein structures were obtained from https://www.rcsb.org/ . The Affinity value, measured in kilocalories per mole, indicates how well the two substances bind together. Higher stability of the ligand-receptor binding results in decreased Affinity (kcal/mol) value.

Samples of HNSCC and normal tissues were collected from patients with HNSCC who were undergoing extensive surgery at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University Medical School. The study conducted adhered to all applicable local, national, and global guidelines. Informed written consent was acquired from all individuals who provided human patient samples prior to donation. Approval for this research was granted by the Human Research Ethics Committee at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine (ethics no. 20240046) (approval date: February 1, 2024).

Each experiment was conducted separately at least three times, and the results were reported as the mean ± SD. Statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.2.1, SPSS version 19.0, and GraphPad 7.0 software. Either the Student’s t test or the Mann-Whitney U test was used to analyze the data from two separate groups. Spearman’s correlation coefficient test was used to evaluate the rank correlations between various variables. Survival differences were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier survival curve, and the significance of the difference in survival time between two groups was assessed with the log rank test. Two-tailed tests were performed on statistical p values, with a significance level of p < 0.05.
sections.results:
CD8A and CD8B encode the α and β chains of CD8 molecules, which play a pivotal role in the immune response mediated by CD8 + T cells. 25 CD8 + T cells represent a diverse population with intricate functional states. Moreover, these subsets of CD8 + T cells exhibit distinct preferences for tissue distribution and demonstrate dynamic properties in TME. 26 Due to such heterogeneity, the assessment of CD8 + T cell infiltration level in previous research using conventional methods lacked accuracy and comprehensiveness, and the expression of CD8A or CD8B did not fully reflect the degree of CD8 + T cell infiltration. The integration of multi-omics approaches based on transcriptome and single-cell data offered us a viable solution. Initially, we assessed the correlation between CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores and prognosis based on single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), Tumor Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion (TIDE), and Cell Type Identification by Estimating Relative Subsets of RNA Transcripts (CIBERSORT) algorithms in the public The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort. Figures 1 A–1C showed that a higher level of CD8 + T cell infiltration indicated a more favorable prognosis for patients with HNSCC. We also found that patients with clinical T1–2, N2–3 stages, and human papillomavirus (HPV) + demonstrated higher CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores based on ssGSEA ( Figures 1 D–1F). The results of further subgroup analysis revealed that patients with higher CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores significantly exhibited more favorable prognosis in different clinical T1–2, N2–3, III–IV stages and HPV + ( Figures 1 G–1J). In terms of the immune characteristics of CD8 + T cell infiltration in HNSCC, we conducted the correlation between different CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores and immune cells via the Mantel test ( Figures 1 K and 1L). The specific coefficients of the corresponding Spearman correlations are shown in Figures S1 A–S1D. The immune cell gene sets were derived from the CIBERSORT ( Figure 1 K) and ssGSEA ( Figure 1 L) algorithms. We found that T cells CD4 + memory activated, M1 macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and immature B cells showed a more positive correlation, whereas T cells CD4 resting memory, M0 macrophages, activated mast cells, and neutrophils showed a more negative correlation.

Identification of CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes

(A–C) Kaplan-Meier curves to show the relationship between CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores and prognosis base on ssGSEA, TIDE, and CIBERSORT in TCGA cohort. (D–F) The relationship between CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores based on ssGSEA and clinical traits (clinical T and N stages and HPV status) in TCGA cohort. (G–J) Kaplan-Meier curves to show the relationship between CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores based on ssGSEA and prognosis in different clinical stages and HPV status patients of TCGA cohort. (K and L) The correlation between CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores based on ssGSEA, TIDE, and CIBERSORT analyses and immune cells via Mantel test. (M) The relationship of 3 traits and 12 modules revealed by the WGCNA. (N) Construction of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks among genes in the purple module. (O) The gene functional enrichment analysis (GO and KEGG analysis) of the purple module.

Subsequently, 4,204 genes showing differential expression (DEGs) were identified between normal and tumor samples using differential expression analysis from TCGA database. WGCNA was used to discover modules of genes related to CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes using TIDE, ssGSEA, and CIBERSORT algorithms based on TCGA DEGs. The results revealed that the Module Eigengenes (ME)greenyellow, MEmagenta, and MEpurple modules were recognized as significantly relevant modules, and the most pertinent purple module comprised a total of 197 CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes ( Figure 1 M). A network of protein-protein interactions (PPIs) was constructed to elucidate the interplay between these genes ( Figures 1 N and S1 K).

We conducted an analysis of Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment to identify the possible biological pathways associated with these genes. The biological functions of the most significant genes were selected for visualization. Key GO terms included control of cell-cell adhesion, T cell activation regulation, T cell growth, binding to cytokine receptors, cytokine function, and binding to chemokine receptors. Furthermore, the KEGG pathway analysis results indicated a significant enrichment of genes in cytokine receptor interaction and chemokine signaling pathway ( Figure 1 O).

Univariate Cox regression analysis of TCGA cohort showed that 33 of 197 CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes were strongly associated with the survival of patients with HNSCC ( Figure 2 A). To gain a deeper understanding of the involvement of CD8 + T cell-associated genes in HNSCC, we performed non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) clustering analysis to categorize patients with cancer in the entire cohort based on the expression levels of 33 genes. The goal of this analysis was to categorize the HNSCC cohort into clusters of cold ( n = 658) and hot tumors ( n = 390) ( Figure 2 B). The intergroup distribution between cold and hot cluster tumors was confirmed to be excellent based on principal-component analysis (PCA) ( Figure 2 C). Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) were employed to confirm the precision of clustering analysis ( Figures S2 C and S2D). Patients with cluster hot tumors had significantly longer overall survival than those with cluster cold tumors, as shown by the Kaplan-Meier survival curves ( p < 0.001) ( Figure 2 D). The proportion of patients with more advanced clinical N stage and HPV + was significantly higher in cluster hot tumors ( Figures 2 E and S3 A). These findings indicate that the HNSCC tumor group can be divided into hot and cold tumor groups, depending on the genes associated with CD8 + T cell infiltration.

Construction of hot and cold clusters for HNSCC-based CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores and identification of significant CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes indicated prognosis in HNSCC

(A) Univariate Cox regression analysis revealed that 33 CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes were significantly correlated with prognosis. (B) Two-CD8 + T cell-related molecular clusters were identified using NMF clustering analysis. (C) The PCA analysis of distinct CD8 + T cell-related molecular clusters. (D) Kaplan-Meier curves showing the difference in overall survival between hot and cold cluster tumors. (E) The heatmap of clinical TNM stages and HPV status between hot and cold cluster tumors. (F) Volcano plot-based DEGs between cluster hot and cold tumors. (G) Heatmap of the relationship between ESTIMATE scores, GSVA, and different cohorts of the two clusters. (H and I) The biological functions based on GO and KEGG enrichment analyses and GSVA between hot and cold cluster tumors. (J) Differences in the pathways-based GSVA between the two clusters. (K–M) Differences in the expression of immune-infiltrating cells and immune-related functions based on ssGSEA (K and L) and CIBERSORT (M) between the two clusters. ∗ p < 0.05; ∗∗ p < 0.01; ∗∗∗ p < 0.001; ∗∗∗∗ p < 0.0001. (N) Flower plot showing overlapping genes (OLR1, SNAPC1, and CLEC10A) based on eight machine learning algorithms. (O–T) Importance of OLR1, SNAPC1, and CLEC10A was assessed using different algorithms. (U) Real-time-qPCR analysis of OLR-1, SNAPC1, and CLEC10A mRNA expression in normal and tumor tissues. (V) Subcellular localization of OLR-1 in A-431 and CACO-2 from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) database. Scale bar, 20 μm. (W) IHC was used to compare OLR1 expression in normal and tumor tissues. Scale bar, 200 μm. ∗ p < 0.05; ∗∗ p < 0.01; ∗∗∗ p < 0.001; ∗∗∗∗ p < 0.0001.

A weighted co-expression network was constructed and displayed as a volcano plot using DEGs based on the two clusters ( Figure 2 F). Subsequently, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were conducted to elucidate the biological functions ( Figure 2 H). The majority of these genes were highly concentrated in the natural killer (NK) cell-mediated cytotoxicity and T cell receptor signaling pathways during GSEA ( Figure 2 I). To characterize the immune environments in the two groups, we generated a heatmap to display the correlation between ‌Estimation of STromal and Immune cells in MAlignant Tumour tissues using Expression data (ESTIMATE) scores, gene set variation analysis (GSVA) scores, and various cohorts ( Figure 2 G). In the GSVA ( Figure 2 J), cluster cold tumors showed greater significance in glycolysis and mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1, Notch, transforming growth factor β, and WNT-β catenin signaling, whereas cluster hot tumors exhibited more significance in apoptosis and interleukin-6-Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (IL-6-JAK-STAT3) signaling. The results showed that the hot tumor cluster had higher immune, stromal, and ESTIMATE scores and lower tumor purity, indicating a more pronounced immune cell infiltration and a better response to immunotherapy in the hot tumor cluster ( Figure S3 B).

Additionally, we employed ssGSEA and CIBERSORT methods to investigate immune cell infiltration levels and immune-related functions in the two clusters. Angiogenesis was identified as a crucial pathway, and a higher abundance of tumor-infiltrating immune cells was observed in the hot tumor cluster using the ssGSEA algorithm ( Figures 2 K and 2L). In cluster hot tumors, immune functions were found to be more hyperactive than in cluster cold tumors, except for dendritic cell and mast cell activation in the CIBERSORT algorithm ( Figure 2 M). The levels of various crucial immune checkpoints (e.g., cytotoxic T lymphocyte associated protein 4 [CTLA-4], PDCD1, LAG-3) and molecules related to the chemokine signaling pathway were significantly elevated in cluster hot tumors compared to cluster cold tumors ( Figures S3 C–S3G). These results suggest that CD8 + T cell-based scores will contribute to the understanding of the molecular mechanisms of HNSCC occurrence and guide the clinical treatment of HNSCC.

Eight machine learning algorithms were employed to identify significant CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes based on 33 prognosis-related genes, including least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, random forest (RF), gradient boosting (GB), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), gradient boosting machine (GBM), extreme GB (XGBoost), and decision tree (DT). Genes with the highest feature rankings as candidate diagnostic genes from these algorithms are shown in Figures S4 A–S4H. Overlapping genes (OLR1, SNAPC1, and CLEC10A) were selected as powerful prognostic factors based on the eight machine learning algorithms mentioned above, and were visualized using a flower plot ( Figure 2 N). The importance of these three genes was further assessed using different algorithms ( Figures 2 O–2T). Finally, we screened the hub prognostic gene, OLR1, which is associated with CD8 + T cell infiltration. RT-qPCR was used to validate the mRNA expression of the three signature genes in both tumor and normal tissues. The results demonstrated that the mRNA expression of the three genes was significantly elevated in tumor tissues ( Figure 2 U), and OLR1 expression in tumor tissues was the highest (3.73 times compared in normal tissues). Subcellular localization of OLR1 in the nucleoplasm and plasma membrane was observed using the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) database ( Figure 2 V). IHC assays of OLR1 expression also showed similar findings, with OLR-1 protein showing a markedly elevated relative expression in tumor tissues compared to that in normal tissues, with a 7-fold increase in quantitative expression ( Figure 2 W). These meaningful results for expression of OLR1 mRNA and protein provide strong evidence for the remarkable role played by OLR1 in HNSCC.

The expression of OLR1 was verified using the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) database (CPTAC database: https://proteomics.cancer.gov/programs/cptac ). As shown in Figure 3 A, the mRNA levels were significantly elevated in tumor samples compared to normal samples, and we also verified that the expression of OLR-1 was significantly higher in tumor tissues in different HNSCC cohorts ( Figures 3 B–3D). We found that high expression of OLR1 was associated with higher histological grades and that the expression of OLR1 in the G1 phase was significantly lower than that in the other groups ( Figure 3 G). In patients with advanced clinical stages and CDH1 mutations, OLR1 was highly expressed ( Figures 3 E, 3F, and 3H). Additionally, higher OLR1 expression was found in patients who exhibited a high response rate to radiotherapy ( Figure 3 I). Kaplan-Meier analysis further supported the association between higher OLR1 expression and unfavorable outcomes of multiple HNSCC cohorts, as shown in Figures 3 J–3N.

Correlations of the OLR1 expression with prognosis and biological functions

(A–D) The expression of OLR1 in tumor tissues and normal tissue from the CPTAC database and different HNSCC cohorts. (E–H) The expression of OLR1 in clinically advanced stages (E and F), histological grades (G), and CDH1 mutation (H). (I) The relationship of OLR1 expression and response rate to radiotherapy. (J–N) Kaplan-Meier curves showing the relationship between OLR1 expression and survival in different HNSCC cohorts. (O and P) GO and KEGG enrichment analyses of gene correlations with OLR1 expression based on Pearson correlation analysis. (Q–W) GSEA of DEGs between the OLR1 high- and low-expression groups.

We selected genes that exhibited positive and negative correlations with OLR1 expression based on Pearson correlation analysis and demonstrated the biological functions of the enriched through by GO and KEGG analyses ( Figures 3 O and 3P). The GO analysis results showed significant enrichment items related to immune system process regulation, response to stimulus regulation, peptide metabolism, and cellular amide metabolism in Biological Process (BP); cell periphery, plasma membrane, and plasma membrane in Cellular Component (CC); and protein binding in Molecular Function (MF). Important KEGG pathways were related to glycan biosynthesis and metabolism, signaling molecules, interaction, and translation. Subsequent GSEA showed that OLR1 was associated with a variety of signaling pathways related to tumor progression, and it was particularly significantly enriched in the inflammatory response, TNF-α-nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) signaling, epithelial mesenchymal transition, IL-6-JAK-STAT3 signaling, IL-2-STAT5 signaling, and the angiogenesis pathway ( Figures 3 Q–3W).

To characterize the diverse single-cell immune profiles of HNSCC, we analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data obtained from the GEO database. In the following analysis, a combined total of 73,475 cells were examined, with 60,608 cells originating from tumor tissues and 12,867 cells from normal tissues. We annotated clusters based on the expression of known marker genes in tissues, including B cells, CD4 + T cells, CD8 + T cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, mast cells, monocytes, neutrophils, NK cells, plasma cells, and regulatory T cells (Tregs) ( Figures 4 A, 4B, and S5 ). Significantly increased numbers of CD8 + T cells, macrophages, neutrophils, NK cells, monocytes, and Tregs were observed in the tumor tissues ( Figure 4 C). In addition, OLR1 expression in HNSCC was significantly higher in macrophages and neutrophils than in other cell clusters ( Figures 4 D and 4E). Using ST data, we employed tissue section projection to demonstrate a wide distribution of macrophages, and we observed an overlapping distribution area between OLR1 and macrophages as well as neutrophils, which aligned with the findings from single-cell analysis ( Figures 4 F and S6 ).

Single-cell expression atlas and tumor-specific signaling pathways in HNSCC tissues

(A) UMAP plots for cell clustering. (B) Bubble plot displaying the expression of representative well-known markers across the cell types identified in HNSCC. (C) The proportion of different cell clusters in normal and tumor tissues. (D and E) The relationship of OLR1 expression and different cell clusters in normal and tumor tissues. (F) The spatial arrangement of OLR1 expression and cell clusters via spatial transcriptomics analysis. (G and K) Circle plots showing an overview of cell-cell interaction numbers and strength among different cell clusters in normal (G) and tumor (K) tissues. (H and L) Bubble plot of several tumor-specific pathways among different cell clusters in normal (H) and tumor (L) tissues. (I and J) MIF and IL-16 signaling network shown via heatmap, violin plot, and circle plot in normal tissues. (M–O) MIF, galectin, and SPP1 signaling network shown via heatmap and violin plot in tumor tissues.

To elucidate the mechanisms underlying cell-cell interactions among these cells, we constructed separate intercellular communication networks among different cell clusters in normal and tumor tissues using the CellChat method. As shown in Figures 4 G and 4H, dendritic cells and monocytes in normal tissues had the most interactions with other stromal and immune cells. Primarily, the macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) and IL-16 signaling networks were present between these cells ( Figures 4 I and 4J). In tumor tissues, we found that most intercellular interactions were significantly enhanced compared to those in normal tissues, especially among CD8 + T cells, macrophages, and neutrophils. We observed that several signaling pathways were primarily present, including the MIF, IL-16, galectin, secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1), chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand, and CCL pathways ( Figures 4 K and 4L). The most robust interactions among CD8 + T cells, macrophages, and neutrophils were the MIF, galectin, and SPP1 pathways ( Figures 4 M–4O). MIF-(CD74 + CD44), LGALS9-CD45, and SPP1-CD44 strongly correlated.

In addition, we performed single-cell analysis using peripheral blood data, including 59,116 cells. The cell cluster and CellChat results are shown in Figures 5 and S7 . OLR1 expression in peripheral blood was still higher in neutrophils, macrophages, and monocytes. We found that intercellular communication networks in peripheral blood were less abundant than those in tissue specimens from patients with tumors and healthy donors. More and stronger signaling pathways between CD8 + T cells and other cells in patients with tumors included the MIF and galectinpathways.

(C) Relationship between OLR-1 expression and different cell clusters in normal and tumor peripheral blood. (D and F) Circle plots showing an overview of cell-cell interaction numbers and strength among different cell clusters in normal (D) and tumor (F) peripheral blood. The single-cell analysis above revealed stronger interaction between macrophages and CD8 + T cells compared to that between neutrophils and CD8 + T cells. To explore more specific cellular subsets interactions, a single-cell expression atlas and interactions between macrophages and CD8 + T cells subsets were constructed. We annotated macrophage subsets in tissues based on the expression of known marker genes, including M0, M1, M2, myofibroblast-like, pro-inflammatory, and Res-like macrophages ( Figures 6 A and 6C). Pseudo-time analysis in HNSCC tissues results showed that M0 and myofibroblast-like macrophages occurred primarily in the upstream of differentiation, progressively diverging into M1 and M2 macrophages. We also observed that the distribution of Res-like macrophages was more extensive and exhibited partial overlap with M1 and M2 macrophages ( Figure 6 D). OLR1 expression in macrophage subsets was significantly higher in M0 macrophages, followed by M1 and Res-like macrophages ( Figures 6 B and 6F). Pseudo-time analysis of OLR-1 projection indicates a decline in OLR1 expression during the differentiation process, with a greater inclination toward cells in the M1 differentiation direction ( Figure 6 E). APOE has been validated as a significant biomarker for tumor-associated macrophages. We observed that OLR1 and APOE were co-expressed in tumor tissues based on public single-cell data ( Figure 6 F). Immunofluorescence was used to further verify OLR1 and APOE co-expression in normal and tumor tissues ( Figure 6 G). We found that a significant upregulation of both OLR1 and APOE in tumor tissues with OLR1 showed more robust expression, exhibiting remarkably similar distribution regions. We also annotated CD8 + T cell subsets in tissues based on the expression of known marker genes, including cycling, cytotoxic, naive-like, pre-dysfunctional, and terminally exhausted CD8 + T cells ( Figures 6 H and 6I). Significantly increased numbers of cycling and terminally exhausted CD8 + T cells were observed in the tumor tissues ( Figure 6 J). An overview of cell-cell interaction and signaling pathways among macrophages and CD8 + T cell subsets is shown in tumor tissues using the CellChat method in Figures 6 K and S8 C. There were more and stronger cell-cell interactions between M0 and M1 macrophages and subsets of CD8 + T cells. The most robust interactions were the MIF, galectin, and SPP1 pathways, manifesting among M0 and M1 macrophages and terminally exhausted, pre-dysfunctional CD8 + T cells ( Figure S8 C).

We annotated macrophages and CD8 + T cell subsets in peripheral blood based on the expression of known marker genes ( Figures 7 A and 7F). Macrophages subsets included M0, M1, M2, NK T-like, pro-inflammatory, and Res-like macrophages ( Figure 7 C). Pseudo-time analysis in tumor peripheral blood did not reveal a distinct differentiation between M1 and M2 macrophages, possibly attributed to low gene expression and diversity of subsets ( Figure 7 D). We also observed that OLR1 expressed more prominently in M0 macrophages as in tumor tissues, and were co-expressed with APOE in tumor peripheral blood ( Figures 7 B and 7E). CD8 + T cells subsets included Naive, NK T-like, Tem GZMK + , Trm, Temra, and human leukocyte antigen-DR isotype-positive (HLA-DR + ) T cells ( Figure 7 G). The proportion of Temra and HLA-DR + T cells was significantly increased in the tumor peripheral blood ( Figure 7 H). We constructed separate intercellular communication networks among macrophages and CD8 + T cell subsets in normal ( Figure S8 F) and tumor ( Figure S8 G) peripheral blood. The signaling pathways in tumor peripheral blood exhibited an increasing intensity, primarily in M0 macrophages ( Figures 7 I–7L). The SPP1 pathway was significantly enhanced in tumor peripheral blood, compared with normal peripheral blood. Overall, the subsets of macrophages and CD8 + T cells exhibited more complexity and diversity in the single-cell profile of peripheral blood compared with that in tissues, although the signaling pathways were comparatively weaker.

The expression of OLR1 was significantly elevated in patients with immune hot scores ( Figure 8 A). Our research focused on examining the correlation between levels of OLR1 expression and the effectiveness of immunotherapy. As illustrated in Figures 8 B–8F, the expression of the most common immune checkpoint genes, especially programmed cell death protein ligand 1 (PD-L1) (CD274), B7-H3 (CD276), and CTLA-4, positively correlated with OLR1 expression. We also observed a notable increase in the expression of OLR1 in patients who demonstrated a favorable response to immunotherapy ( Figures 8 G and 8H). The AUC of the OLR1 expression level model for predicting an effective response to immunotherapy were 0.745, 0.788, 0.776, and 0.750 for the multiple HNSCC immunotherapy cohorts, respectively ( Figures 8 I–8L). In addition, patients with elevated level of OLR1 expression exhibited extended survival rates in various immunotherapy cohorts for HNSCC ( Figures 8 M–8P).

The correlation between OLR1 gene expression and drug responsiveness was examined using information from two drug sensitivity repositories, the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) and Clinical Trials Reporting Program (CTRP), accessed through the GSCALite web platform. This study investigated the potential clinical uses of the overexpression and related roles of the OLR1 gene in HNSCC. These findings indicated a significant correlation between OLR1 expression and sensitivity to various targeted drugs ( Figures 8 Q and 8R). Additionally, computational molecular docking simulations were conducted to investigate the interactions between the correlated drugs and OLR1 protein. The drug sensitivity analysis revealed pazopanib and simvastatin to be highly sensitive inhibitors of OLR1. Subsequently, we conducted molecular docking studies to confirm the binding efficacy of OLR1 with these two drugs ( Figures 8 S and 8T). The side chains of pazopanib (−7.329 kcal/mol) formed hydrogen bonds with GLU A:218 and SER A:207, and hydrophobic interactions with ARG A:209 and LEU A:216. The side chains of simvastatin (−6.263 kcal/mol) formed hydrophobic interactions with PHE A:202, PHE A:261, and PHE A:200.
sections.discussion:
In HNSCC clinical practice, conventional tumor therapies (local surgical removal, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy) generally result in trauma, postoperative facial deformity, and a high rate of recurrence. The efficacy of current targeted therapy limited by tumor heterogeneity was also unfavorable. 27 The treatment of HNSCC has undergone a paradigm shift with the advent of cancer immunotherapy, particularly targeting immune checkpoints, such as PD-1 or CTLA-4 inhibitors, which exhibited the most significant clinical activity. 8 However, the effectiveness of immunotherapies is influenced by various resistance mechanisms, including immune exclusion, immune editing, reduced antigen presentation, and immune suppression through cellular mechanisms. 28 , 29 These dynamics necessitated a more comprehensive investigation into the intricate interactions among various cells in the TME, which could be implemented by omics technology. CD8 + T cells act as the major cells that fight tumors in the TME, primarily working as cells that destroy other cells. Nevertheless, their functionality is hindered by suppressive cell populations and molecules that modulate the response of the immune system. 13 Therefore, gaining a thorough understanding of CD8 + T cell regulation within the TME and finding novel biomarkers are of great importance for patients with HNSCC.

Our study demonstrated a significant correlation between the favorable prognosis of HNSCC and the extent of CD8 + T cell infiltration, as quantified by CD8 + T cell infiltration scores. This finding aligns with observations in other malignant tumors. 30 , 31 A novel CD8 + T cell-associated prognostic model was developed in bladder cancer to identify patients who would derive greater benefit from immunotherapy, which was further validated using a real-world immunotherapy cohort. 31 Jin et al. reported a notable increase in CD8 + T cells within a specific cohort, which was associated with improved outcomes in tongue squamous cell carcinoma. 32 Previous study also found that inducing a heightened degree of CD8 + T cell infiltration in the rabbit liver tumor model resulted in the deceleration of tumor growth and the promotion of tumor necrosis. 33 These findings have the potential to contribute toward the implementation of CD8 + T cell infiltration-related scores for predicting the survival of HNSCC patients. A large number of studies have demonstrated that the tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging system and HPV status are significant factors influencing prognosis and treatment decisions for HNSCC patients. 3 , 4 , 5 Varying levels of CD8 + T cell infiltration among patients with different TNM stages in HNSCC, which was primarily influenced by clinical T stage. 34 A retrospective analysis found that significantly extended survival was observed when there was high infiltration of T lymphocytes, along with HPV positivity in HNSCC. 35 Our analysis additionally demonstrated that patients with a more advanced clinical N stage and those who were HPV + exhibited increased levels of CD8 + T cell infiltration. Furthermore, elevated CD8 + T cell infiltration was associated with improved prognosis in specific clinical subgroups. These findings suggest that further analysis of clinical subgroups could inform the development of future personalized therapeutic strategies based on CD8 + T cell infiltration.

WGCNA demonstrates superior predictive accuracy and efficiency in detecting genes with comparable expression profiles compared to other methods. 36 We applied WGCNA to accurately select significant CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes and further classified the HNSCC tumor cohort into hot and cold tumor groups based on CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes related to prognosis. We also observed a higher proportion of advanced N stage and HPV + patients in the hot tumor group, indicating that these patients may gain survival benefits through immune checkpoint blockades. 37 This indicates that HNSCC is one of the cancer types with the most significant infiltration of CD8 + T cells, highlighting the crucial role of CD8 + T cell infiltration-related genes in immune response and surveillance. We employed various machine learning techniques to decrease the number of variables and improve the accuracy of predicting the prognosis of HNSCC. Finally, we screened the hub gene OLR1, which was most closely associated with prognosis in HNSCC.

OLR1, a lectin-like receptor for oxidized low-density lipoproteins, is widely expressed in mammals and can bind to different molecules. It is found in macrophages, endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, platelets, and neurons in Homo sapiens . Extensive research has been conducted on the connection between atherosclerosis and other vascular conditions, such as hypertension and stroke. 38 , 39 Recently, the overexpression of OLR1 has been observed to be linked to the increased activity of multiple cancer-causing genes, cell death, and growth in different cancer types, contributing to disease progression. 40 , 41 , 42 Our research revealed a strong correlation between elevated OLR1 levels in HNSCC and higher histological grade, more advanced clinical stage, and worse prognosis, and further verified OLR1 expression through RT-qPCR and IHC staining. The knockdown of OLR1 could result in a decrease in the expression of OLR1 and Ki67 by western blot analysis, and colon cancer growth rate and weight in nude mice. 43 It also has been verified through in vivo and in vitro experiments that OLR1 could modulate the autophagic network to govern esophageal cancer cell proliferation. 44 GSEA revealed significant enrichments of OLR1 high expression in the pathways related to promoting tumor occurrence and development, angiogenesis, and immunosuppression, such as TNF-α-NF-κB signaling and IL-2-STAT5 signaling. Liang et al. also noted that the upregulation of endothelial OLR1 is induced by TNF-α, thereby promoting the adhesion and transendothelial migration of MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. 45 A sustained elevation of IL-2 levels was reported to promote 5-hydroxytryptophan production through the STAT5-TPH1 pathway, ultimately causing dysfunctionality among CD8 + T cells within the TME. 46 The expression of OLR1 was also found to be significantly elevated in patients with HNSCC and immune hot score and high level of immune checkpoint gene expression. Some publicly available immunotherapy cohorts revealed that patients exhibiting high OLR1 expression demonstrated a superior response to immunotherapy, suggesting the possibility of utilizing OLR1 expression as a promising and accurate marker to predict the rate of immune response in HNSCC, which has not been reported in the literature. In molecular docking analysis based on drug sensitivity, pazopanib and simvastatin showed the best binding activity with OLR1. This necessitates further investigation in clinical trials. These results demonstrated the potential value of OLR1 in early diagnosis, prediction of prognosis, and immune response of HNSCC.

Using single-cell analysis of tissue specimens and peripheral blood, we elucidated the composition of the TME landscape in HNSCC. OLR1 expression in HNSCC was significantly elevated in neutrophils, macrophages, and monocytes. Then, we found multiple signaling pathways, such as MIF, galectin, and SPP1 pathways between CD8 + T cells and other myeloid immune cells. These signaling pathways played a pivotal role in various processes associated with cancer development, including angiogenesis, metastasis, proliferation of cancer cells, and invasiveness. 47 , 48 , 49 The findings of Zheng et al. demonstrated that galectin-9 (Gal-9), triggered by stimulator of interferon (IFN) genes/IFN-β communication, was a key factor in cancer cells escaping the immune system, presenting a promising target for cancer treatment through immunotherapy. This study proposed a novel approach combining anti-Gal-9 with existing therapies to treat a range of cancers, even those that did not respond to current treatments like PD-1/PD-L1 blockade therapy. 50 It was reported that the close proximity of SPP1 + macrophages, CD8 + T cells, and CD4 + T cells in breast cancer with high levels of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and hormone receptor positivity was revealed by ST data, which provided valuable insights for targeted interventions. 51

In further single-cell subsets atlas and interactions based on OLR1 expression, we also observed substantial and extensive cell-cell interactions among M0 and M1 macrophages and terminally exhausted, pre-dysfunctional CD8 + T cells. We found that OLR1 expression was significantly higher in M0 macrophages, and we confirmed the co-expression of OLR1 and APOE in tumor tissues through immunofluorescence. APOE is an arginine-rich protein that is involved in regulating lipid metabolism, Alzheimer disease, and other pathological conditions. 52 , 53 , 54 The co-expression of OLR1 and APOE in malignant tumors has not been reported in the literature. In recent years, APOE + macrophages have been identified in different malignant tumors, elucidating their pivotal role in the prediction of molecular subtyping, prognosis, and immunotherapy response. 55 , 56 The interaction and increased distance between APOE + macrophages and terminally exhausted CD8 + T cells were confirmed through multiple IHC procedures, which exerted an influence on the response to ICIs. 57 A previous study found that OLR1 staining specifically localized to CD68 + tumor-associated macrophages in HNSCC samples and OLR1 expression level served as a reliable indicator for evaluating the infiltration of tumor-associated macrophages, with its prognostic significance is tumor-specific. 58 The above results suggest that the potential involvement of OLR1 in macrophage development and differentiation in HNSCC and OLR1 and APOE might regulate CD8 + T cell infiltration through signaling pathways between CD8 + T cells and macrophages. Further studies are required to elucidate the exact molecular mechanisms involved. Moreover, the results of single-cell analysis in peripheral blood also exhibited similar cell-cell interactions and pathways as results in tissue specimens. This means that we could analyze OLR1 expression by noninvasive and reproducible detection. 59

In the thriving landscape of emerging biomaterials and nanotechnology, meticulously designed targeted nanoparticle systems have been engineered to enhance drug delivery efficacy. The drug delivery of nanomaterials exhibits the characteristics of targeted delivery, enhanced permeability and retention, improved bioavailability, reduced toxicity, and evasion of the reticuloendothelial system. 60 , 61 , 62 It was verified that drug-loaded exosomes delivered by glypican-3-targeted macrophages exerted antitumor immune effects through a variety of pathways. 63 Our enthusiastic perspective is founded on the integration of biomaterials and biomedicine for strategic interventions targeting OLR1-associated macrophages and regulating CD8 + T cell infiltration in TME, enhancing the effectiveness of clinical interventions and improving the prognosis of HNSCC patients.
